items.title: China’s conspicuous absence in Asian energy security plans
items.summary: As Asian leaders plan for regional energy security cooperation, China's focus is elsewhere, while Japan is stepping up. The post China’s conspicuous absence in Asian energy security plans appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis notes China is largely absent from Asian energy security cooperation plans while Japan steps up.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Asia's energy security is being reshaped by the Strait of Hormuz disruption, which has pushed importers to diversify suppliers, energy mix and trade routes. They contend China, the region's largest oil importer and stockpiler, is largely absent from new regional energy security planning, and that its export restrictions and limited transparency have harmed neighbours. Japan is positioned as the lead architect, through POWERR Asia, a proposed Asian oil security task force, and the POWERR Gulf initiative with joint stockpiling arrangements with Gulf national oil companies. The authors caution that these fossil-fuel-heavy frameworks may clash with Southeast and South Asian preferences for electrification and renewables, and that China's clean-energy strengths remain an untapped asset.
brief.argument: China's domestic-first energy choices and opacity leave a gap in Asian energy security planning that Japan is well placed to fill, though the proposed frameworks may be too fossil-fuel focused.
recommendations: Use Gulf-Japan joint stockpiling as a template for other nations under POWERR Gulf
Direct scarce resources toward electrification, renewables, battery storage and grid resilience rather than new fossil infrastructure
Engage China in regional energy cooperation despite its current reluctance
Diversify supplier relationships, energy mix and trade routes away from Middle Eastern dependence

items.title: Global climate governance is fragmenting. But plurilateralism can keep cooperation alive.
items.summary: As geopolitical divisions undermine global climate negotiations, smaller coalitions of like-minded countries are finding ways to keep climate cooperation moving. The post Global climate governance is fragmenting. But plurilateralism can keep cooperation alive. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues smaller coalitions of like-minded countries are keeping climate cooperation alive amid fragmentation.

brief.summary: The author argues that global climate governance is fragmenting as the COP31 talks in Antalya ended without consensus over fossil-fuel phaseouts and climate finance, with the US absent after leaving the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. Rather than signalling the end of cooperation, countries are turning to smaller like-minded coalitions outside the consensus-based COP process. The piece points to Brazil's voluntary fossil-fuel and deforestation roadmap, Türkiye's non-binding '35 by 35' electrification pledge, and the Colombia-Netherlands conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels. The author holds that plurilateralism can produce practical solutions and build momentum, but cannot replace multilateral action or mobilise the concessional and private finance developing countries need. The test, in the authors' view, is whether such coalitions turn declarations into delivery.
brief.argument: Climate cooperation is shifting from consensus-based COP negotiations toward plurilateral coalitions of willing countries, which can advance practical action but cannot substitute for multilateral finance and commitment.
recommendations: Use plurilateral coalitions to develop practical solutions, common standards and financing arrangements that can later feed into wider agreements
Mobilise substantial concessional public finance and effective risk-sharing mechanisms, since private capital alone will not close the adaptation gap
Ensure voluntary initiatives include mechanisms to track follow-through on commitments
brief.turkey: Türkiye, as COP31 co-host, championed the non-binding '35 by 35' electrification pledge and the BRIDGE implementation platform, which the piece treats as examples of plurilateral progress.

items.title: Why Taiwan’s Local Elections Matter for Deterring China
items.summary: As gray zone pressure from China grows, local resilience efforts will play a critical role in the island’s response to an emergency. That will matter for the United States, too.

ai.sum: CFR analysis argues that Taiwan's local elections and resilience efforts matter for deterring Chinese gray zone pressure.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Taiwan's ability to withstand Chinese gray-zone pressure, quarantine or blockade depends heavily on local governments, which translate national Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience priorities into budgets, sheltering, evacuation planning, stockpiles and communications continuity. They point to Taiwan's Urban Resilience exercises, which tested mutual aid between jurisdictions and civil-military coordination, and to Beijing's growing cyber intrusions and disinformation during local elections. They note the Taipei mayoral race is entangled with civil defence, since a DPP candidate linked to a leading civil preparedness NGO was placed under investigation by Chinese authorities. The authors frame local resilience as a factor in Beijing's calculus, and argue that Washington should support civilian institutions and city-to-city exchanges, not only military sales, because such cooperation is politically less sensitive.
brief.argument: Local governments' resilience capacity will shape both Taiwan's ability to survive coercion and Beijing's decision to attempt it, so the United States should invest in Taiwan's civilian institutions and local partnerships.
recommendations: Share expertise with Taiwan on emergency communications, disaster response, community preparedness and continuity of government
Encourage city-to-city cooperation that matches the scale of local jurisdictions
Treat civil resilience cooperation as a lower-sensitivity complement to defence cooperation

ai.sum: An industry firm describes running an accelerator day to press the Pentagon's Special Operations office to meet procurement deadlines.
actors: Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Ope

brief.summary: The authors, two US Department of Defense acquisition officials, describe an accelerator day held on July 24 for the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict. They argue that a short, deadline-driven process, using legally binding awards of $10,000 per finalist and $50,000 seed funding for ten, can put the government under pressure to decide. They present a portfolio approach: start small, test operationally, and commit larger sums only when evidence justifies it. They acknowledge risks, including unresolved transition funding, limited operator access, and the gap between prototype awards and fielding. Three months on, two projects were moved to other pathways and four have funded operational demonstrations. The piece frames the next test as sustaining urgency through assessment and adoption, not just award speed.
brief.argument: Rapid, bounded prototype awards can force timely government decisions, but only if the government sustains ownership and funding through operational assessment and adoption.
recommendations: Keep a named government owner and resolution date for every assessment delayed by funding, stakeholder agreement or operator access.
Commit larger funding only after operational evidence shows a capability merits it, and avoid repeated small pilots that delay fielding.
Engage potential adopters such as military services or foreign partners early so assessments produce the evidence they need to invest.
Be prepared to stop efforts honestly when operational demand or support no longer justifies them.

items.title: Does Congress Really Want Its War Powers Back?
items.summary: Congress wants its war powers back. At least, that is the message that the legislature has communicated to the public numerous times over the past decade. Members of Congress have forced an astonishing number of votes on resolutions challenging unauthorized presidential warmaking, with some achieving historically unprecedented success in one or both chambers of Congress. But soon, it will become time for Congress to put its money where its mouth is. In its flurry of Vietnam…

ai.sum: An analysis questions whether Congress truly wants to reclaim its war powers from the presidency despite repeated resolution votes.

brief.summary: The author, Elizabeth Beavers, argues that Congress has repeatedly used privileged war powers resolutions since the Chadha ruling, with Iran-related resolutions dominating under Trump, but that these votes are largely symbolic because presidential vetoes block them. She notes stronger tools exist, such as funding restrictions, lawsuits by Congress as an institution, and statutory reform like sunsetting the 2001 AUMF. She contends that congressional behaviour is best explained not by partisanship or a desire to reclaim constitutional powers, but by a deep bipartisan commitment to U.S. global primacy, which makes Congress tolerate executive overreach that serves that aim and resist it only when a president appears to retrench. The piece treats the coming Democratic-led Congress as a test of whether its rhetoric about reclaiming war powers will be matched by action.
brief.argument: Congress's repeated war powers resolutions are largely performative, and its willingness to constrain the president depends on whether he is deviating from a bipartisan commitment to U.S. global primacy rather than on a genuine wish to reclaim constitutional authority.
recommendations: Use appropriations riders to restrict funding for unauthorized military operations against Iran.
Authorise a lawsuit by Congress as an institution to test its standing on war powers questions.
Sunset the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force.
Enact comprehensive reform such as the National Security Powers Act, including approval-based rather than disapproval-based mechanisms.

ai.sum: Analysis says the Shenzhen summit gave Putin equal-standing recognition in a US-China-Russia format and urges Europe to seek a diplomatic seat.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Shenzhen summit between Putin, Xi and Trump gave Moscow a photo opportunity and a vague declaration that should not be mistaken for a breakthrough. They contend the declaration normalises a US-China-Russia format discussing peace, energy, justice and nuclear risk without Europe or Ukraine. Its wording on UN reform, energy flows and nuclear-risk reduction lacks timetables or verification. The piece urges European governments to treat the summit as a warning, insist that Europe and Ukraine be principals in any talks on European security, offer a detailed counter-agenda, and coordinate through the EU and NATO to resist divide-and-rule. It concludes the summit shows Putin is still eager for a new Yalta.
brief.argument: The Shenzhen summit gave Putin great-power recognition through a vague declaration, and Europe must refuse a format that treats Europe and Ukraine as objects rather than participants.
recommendations: Insist that European states and Ukraine are principals in any discussion affecting European security
Offer a detailed counter-agenda on UN reform, energy security, international justice and nuclear-risk reduction
Coordinate positions through the EU and NATO to prevent Moscow dealing with capitals separately
Avoid rewarding Chinese arsenal expansion while including China in nuclear-risk dialogue

items.title: Russia's New Cruise Missiles and the Rapid Iteration Trap
items.summary: Russia’s jet-powered mini cruise missiles outpaced Ukraine’s cheap interceptor drones. Rapid iteration matters, but speed ultimately depends on sovereign engineering capability built over years.

ai.sum: Analysis argues Russia's jet-powered mini cruise missiles outpaced Ukraine's cheap interceptor drones, stressing sovereign engineering capability.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russia's new jet-powered mini cruise missiles (Geran 3, 4, 5 and others such as Banderol, Dan-T and Filin) exposed the limits of Ukraine's fast, iterative procurement model. Ukraine's cheap propeller-drone interceptors, which had become the focus of air defence innovation, were quickly outpaced because Russia moved several iteration cycles ahead. The authors contend that Russia's apparent leap was in fact the product of years of state-backed engineering, including a first mini turbine prototype in 2018 and efforts since 2020 to localise production and reduce reliance on Chinese commercial engines. Their conclusion is that rapid iteration depends on sovereign engineering capacity built over time, and that the UK should strengthen its mini-turbine base and coordinate its R&D efforts.
brief.argument: Rapid iteration is valuable, but sustained speed depends on sovereign engineering capability built over years, as Russia's jet mini cruise missile programme shows.
recommendations: Harness sovereign engineering capability and a ready pool of skilled people in industrial clusters that can be mobilised quickly.
Rebuild neglected UK mini-turbine production capacity.
Use new bodies such as National Armaments Innovation to bring together disparate UK R&D efforts.
Pair fast acquisition with a more methodical approach to unlock speed when it is most needed.

items.title: The Father of Realism and the Purpose of Power
items.summary: We Discuss: Mentioned on the Episode: E. H. Carr, The Twenty Years’ Crisis: 1919–1939, Macmillan Hans J. Morgenthau, In Defense of the National Interest, Alfred A. Knopf Hans J. Morgenthau, Politics Among Nations: The Struggle for Power and Peace, Alfred A. Knopf Hans J. Morgenthau, The Purpose of American Politics, Alfred A. Knopf Hans J. […]

ai.sum: A CFR podcast episode discusses the realist thought of E. H. Carr and Hans Morgenthau.

brief.summary: The authors (a CFR podcast episode, host James Lindsay and guest David Sacks) examine Hans Morgenthau, the founding figure of modern classical realism in international relations. They trace his formative experience of antisemitism and Nazi rise in Coburg, his early critique of American liberal optimism in Scientific Man versus Power Politics, and his opposition to the Vietnam War, including his public clashes with Henry Kissinger. They stress that realism offers no simple policy manual: its fundamental claim that states act in anarchic, self-interested competition must be translated through judgments about vital interests and statesmanship. They present Morgenthau's distinction between status quo and revisionist powers as central to deciding whether accommodation or confrontation is appropriate, and raise the question of whether China today is a revisionist or status quo power.
brief.argument: Realism's core insight about power and self-interest is widely accepted, but turning it into specific policy depends on prudent judgment about vital interests and the intentions of other powers, which Morgenthau treated as essential.
recommendations: Define the national interest in terms of a hierarchy of vital interests rather than universal commitments.
Distinguish status quo powers, which can be accommodated, from revisionist powers, which should be checked.
Rely on the judgment and prudence of statesmen rather than fixed formulas.

ai.sum: ECFR argues the EU's six largest states should cooperate through regional forums to lead the energy transition away from fossil fuels.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Europe remains too dependent on fossil fuels, especially gas in buildings, industry and transport, and that the EU lacks a binding phase-out target. They note the EU's 2040 emissions goal and Russian gas ban, but say member states still pursue fragmented national approaches. Their central proposal is that the EU's six largest economies (France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain) should use existing regional forums such as the Three Seas Initiative, Weimar Triangle, Visegrad Group, MED9 and Pentalateral Forum to coordinate and move Europe from the IEA's current-policies scenario towards its stated-policies scenario. brief.argument: The big six should use regional, intra-EU forums to build a collective fossil-fuel phase-out roadmap, shifting Europe from the IEA's current-policies path to the stated-policies path.
recommendations: Use participation in regional intra-EU forums to find common ground on energy policy among the big six.
Help the more adaptive member states adopt transformative measures that reduce fossil demand.

items.title: The Coast Guard offers a model for defending US critical infrastructure against cyberattacks
items.summary: When it comes to cybersecurity, maritime transportation is arguably the most comprehensively governed of all US critical infrastructure sectors. The post The Coast Guard offers a model for defending US critical infrastructure against cyberattacks appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues the US Coast Guard's maritime cybersecurity governance could serve as a model for protecting other US critical infrastructure.

brief.summary: The authors argue that US maritime transportation is the most comprehensively governed critical infrastructure sector for cybersecurity, and that the Coast Guard's model should be emulated elsewhere. They describe how the Coast Guard combines regulatory authority, law enforcement powers, intelligence community membership and close industry collaboration, including mandatory cybersecurity plans and minimum hygiene rules for covered vessels and facilities. They cite Cyber Protection Teams that assess private networks at industry request, and recent interventions on hacked tankers. The piece then calls for faster incident-reporting rules under CIRCIA, renewal of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act before its December expiry, restoration of CISA's capacity, and a streamlined route to bring US Cyber Command capabilities into serious domestic incidents. It also suggests possible federal regulation with liability insurance requirements, drawing an analogy to post-Exxon Valdez oil rules.
brief.argument: The Coast Guard's blend of regulation, authority and industry partnership offers a template that other US critical infrastructure sectors should adopt for cyber defense.
recommendations: Finalise the CIRCIA incident-reporting rule without delay.
Congress should renew the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act before it expires.
Restore CISA's resources and install a Senate-confirmed director.
Consider federal cyber regulation with liability coverage requirements for private operators.

brief.argument: Ukraine's battlefield-tested drone innovation has made it a global leader in drone warfare, and expanded support for its domestic drone industry is the most realistic path to pressing Russia toward peace.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues the US president and Congress must forge a bipartisan strategy on ending Russia's war against Ukraine.

brief.summary: The author, Matthew H. Murray, argues that a divided US government will prolong Russia's war against Ukraine and invite further aggression. He contends the president and Congress should align their constitutional powers rather than contest them. The proposed mechanism is an Advisory Council on Peace and Security in Ukraine, bringing together the president with bipartisan leaders of the key foreign policy, intelligence and armed services committees. He says the current diplomacy, with envoys Kushner and Witkoff acting as mediators, has failed to halt the fighting and often defers to Russian maximalist demands. The missing element, in his view, is the deterrent effect of combining American military, intelligence, economic and diplomatic power. He argues the Senate's advice-and-consent role can strengthen negotiating leverage and ensure any settlement has durable legal and bipartisan backing.
brief.argument: A bipartisan, structured US strategy that unites presidential diplomacy with congressional authority is needed to raise the costs of Russian aggression and secure a durable end to the war in Ukraine.
recommendations: Establish regular structured consultations between the president and bipartisan leaders of the foreign policy, intelligence and armed services committees, via an Advisory Council on Peace and Security
Use the council to build a consensus on the purpose and role of military assistance to Ukraine.
Use the council to settle negotiating issues, including future security guarantees and when to raise or lift sanctions.
Use the Senate's advice-and-consent role to set clear limits against concessions that undermine US and Ukrainian security.

brief.summary: The authors argue that China has become a lifeline for Russia's defence industry, and that Russian firms are seeking to offshore dual-use production, such as CNC machine tools, to China. They use the case of sanctioned Stankomashstroy, which pursued a plant in Xianyang despite its designation, to illustrate the problem. They contend the incoming US Congress can raise costs for Chinese enablers through sanctions and export-control legislation, such as reviving the STOP China and Russia Act, while leaving the White House diplomatic room. They acknowledge limits: Chinese retaliation via rare earths, the risk of secondary sanctions on banks alienating allies, and the fact that Congress cannot force Beijing to abandon Moscow. They stress that Washington should build allied economic-security coordination to make such leverage credible.
brief.argument: Congress should target Chinese support for Russia's defence industry's offshored dual-use production, using sanctions and export controls that the White House can accept, backed by allied coordination.
recommendations: Revive the STOP China and Russia Act of 2025 to codify sanctions on Russian defence industry enablers in China.
Target Chinese support for Russian overseas production of dual-use technologies such as CNC machine tools.
Build a binding economic security alliance with European and Asian allies to withstand Chinese coercion and coordinate responses.
Hold Beijing to its stated commitment to a Ukraine peace role, so that it cannot present itself as a neutral broker while supplying Russia.

items.summary: China, India, the US, and Bangladesh all have roles to play in ensuring that the recent International Court of Justice verdict helps the Rohingya. The post The Rohingya genocide ruling faces a geopolitical test appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis examines how China, India, the US and Bangladesh could help implement the ICJ ruling on the Rohingya genocide case.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the ICJ's first state-responsibility finding for genocide, against Myanmar over the Rohingya, will be undermined unless its restitution measures, especially access to citizenship, are carried into the political deals that outside powers strike with Myanmar's government and the Arakan Army. They note the court stopped short of ordering full citizenship, so implementation depends on negotiations in which the US (rare earths), China (Kyaukphyu port) and India (Kaladan corridor) have commercial stakes. They describe Bangladesh, which hosts over a million refugees, as already engaging both Naypyidaw and the Arakan Army, and as considering the UN General Assembly, which it presides over, as a platform for coalition-building. They also argue that India's restrained response and the US and Chinese priorities show great-power interests pulling against the verdict, and that the Rohingya must be included in any dialogue.
brief.argument: Without citizenship and safe return built into any settlement, the ICJ ruling will remain unimplemented and another exodus becomes more likely, so outside powers should use their leverage to make it part of the deal.
recommendations: Outside powers should use trade and other leverage to make implementation of the ICJ ruling and a path to citizenship and safe return part of any settlement they support.
Bangladesh should use the UN General Assembly, where it holds the rotating presidency, to build a coalition pressing Myanmar and the Arakan Army to carry out the restitution measures.
Bangladesh should expand border trade with Rakhine as an incentive for cooperation on repatriation.
Rohingya representatives and youth should take part in negotiations on citizenship rights and repatriation.

The author, founder of a wargame grading platform, argues such a test must be valid, repeatable and comparable across services, and that wargaming has little published evidence it can meet these standards. He reports that off-the-shelf large language model graders gave inconsistent, inflated scores, and that a grader built on separated feedback, evidence citation and explicit level standards improved but still passed only two of six proposed tests. brief.argument: Wargames can be turned into valid, repeatable and comparable measures of officer judgment only if the assessment focuses on reasoning, uses rigorous evidence-based grading, and is validated before it influences promotion.
recommendations: Grade the reasoning behind decisions and focus on strategic judgment rather than game outcomes.

brief.summary: The authors argue that artificial intelligence creates a "double alignment problem" on top of the classic civil-military problem: aligning the state with its military and aligning human principals with AI agents. Drawing on Huntington's "objective control" and Feaver's principal-agent framing, they contend that AI undermines the constitutionalism and professionalism that sustain US civil-military relations. They find that Anthropic's "constitution" for Claude is a statement of values rather than binding rules, and that its sovereignty is opaque compared with the transparent multi-principal US constitutional system. They propose a system message or a military-specific behavioural specification, a shift of officer expertise toward strategy and embodied judgement, self-policing of corporateness, and a congressional oversight body on the model of the 1946 Atomic Energy Act to govern military AI.
brief.argument: AI adds an agent-alignment problem to civil-military relations that threatens constitutional control and military professionalism, and it needs rule-based, publicly legitimate governance rather than lab-set values.

They also flag legal professional privilege as a contested issue. Their recommendations include publishing fee principles, defining key terms in secondary legislation, setting minimum agreement terms with professional bodies, certifying readiness before each transfer, explaining risk-rating methods, and piloting an independent procedure for privilege disputes, with the order of decisions mattering as much as content.
brief.argument: Consolidating UK AML supervision of the professions under the FCA is the right call, but the Bill alone will not improve supervision unless the unresolved design, transition and privilege questions are settled first.

brief.summary: The authors, through James M. Lindsay's essay, argue that General William Westmoreland's November 1967 National Press Club speech, given at President Johnson's request, gave an overly optimistic picture of the Vietnam War. They trace how the Americanization of the war failed to break the battlefield deadlock, how rising casualties and a shift in public opinion pressured Johnson, and how the administration chose to shore up support through favourable messaging rather than a clear change of course. The piece presents the Tet Offensive of January 1968 as exposing that rosy picture, contributing to Johnson's decision not to seek reelection. The lesson drawn is that shielding the public from unpleasant realities about overseas military operations can backfire on a president.
brief.argument: Westmoreland's overly upbeat 1967 public assessment of the Vietnam War, made to shore up political support, was discredited by the Tet Offensive and helped undermine Johnson's presidency.
